thread.title: Should You Bet On The Resilience Of The U.S. Economy?

author: Nicholas Kitonyi
title: Should You Bet On The Resilience Of The U.S. Economy?
text:
The US economy has been the best performing among the world’s largest economies. This has fueled investor optimism thereby rallying stock market prices to record highs. However, some things appear to have changed over the last few months with stock prices remaining volatile amid a series of mixed US economic data.
The bull market peaked late last year extending to the start of 2018, but since late January, the market movement has been choppy. Some analysts have pointed to the potential impact of last year’s rally saying it could have led to a minor correction in February. Others have expressed fears of another market crash potentially coming within the next few quarters.
Of course, it isn’t even a decade since the last global financial crises wrecked economies. This means that even with the US showing great recovery, the rest of the world especially developed economies are yet to reach the same heights. This could prove problematic in the near future.
Some like Japan and the EU are employing various economic stimulation measures to overcome recent GDP slowdowns while others like the UK seem too cautious to take the bold step of raising the base interest rate.
The US used quantitative easing (QE), which is basically debt to stimulate economic recovery and several other countries are taking the same measures. When you look at the historical US debt , the government has used private and foreign financing options to fund public projects and bail struggling parastatals and allied organizations in a bid to stimulating economic growth. It can be argued that the US economy is now enjoying the same fruits following the QE before tapering.
Over the last couple of years, the US has taken key measures to showcase the strength of its economic growth.
Since the US started Tapering, it has made key milestones during the recovery Since December 2015, the Federal Reserve has hiked the Funds rate on six occasions to bring it up to the current level of 1.75%. The country’s economic growth has also benefited from falling unemployment rate which has plummeted to about 3.9% from a high of 10% in 2009. The inflation rate, which had proven to be a major stumbling block failing to reach Fed’s targeted 2% recently surpassed this key level again justifying the government body’s approach to interest rates. The US has also enjoyed strong non-farm payrolls numbers, with the number of new jobs created increasing by hundreds of thousands month after month. Furthermore, locally based companies have benefited from the government's adjustments in the monetary policy that included lowering corporate taxes to allow multinational companies like Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) to increase productivity within the US by localizing most of their operations Most multinationals had been reporting a huge chunk of their revenues in tax-friendly countries like The Republic of Ireland, but now more tax revenues could be booked in the US Treasury following the changes in corporate tax. But is the US economy immune to global slowdown? Could external economic slowdown hurt the progress the US economy has shown? Some suggest that it is highly unlikely, but realists know that the US economy is not an island. And even as the government continues to implement tough policies on international trade relations, not everything plays in favor of the US
Recently, the Trump administration announced that 1,333 Chinese products will be hit with punitive tariffs in a move that fulfills President Trump’s promise of protecting local companies. In response to this, Beijing announced that it would impose similar tariffs at 25% penalties on 106 American made products. Interestingly, according to an article published by Financial Times , the damage would be more on the US than it is on China once implemented.
So, this shows that in as much as the US is trying to limit its reliance on foreign economies, there is a long way to go before investors can presume it to be significantly immune from the slowdown in the economies of other world superpowers.
So, what does this mean to investors? The allure of a rapidly growing economy is hard to ignore, especially if that economy also enjoys the stability that comes with being a global superpower. That is the case of the US economy.
As such, over the last couple of years, investors have rallied stocks to new all-time highs. And to talk of all-time highs when we know very well that we just had the global financial crises less than a decade ago, then it shows how rapidly stock prices have skyrocketed.
The nature of this meteoric rise is compounded when you think that it beats the market boom of the early-to-mid 2000s. We all know how that ended a few years later.
So, the question is, have investors rallied stocks too much than the US economy can handle? Some experts have speculated that the February slide was potentially an indication that the market is due a major correction. Others linked the sell-off to the cryptocurrency market as cryptocurrency prices plummeted. Both camps might be correct.
However, the market has recovered over the last few months, which raises the initial question of whether the correction is still on the horizon. If it comes, it could be catastrophic for investors who bought the rally late last year.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
